title: How Fats corrected stock arrangements in the studio
summary: Players got stock parts or lead sheets at the session, and Fats would explode at wrong bass notes, rewrite the part and tell each man what to play.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: That's it. You know, these things that you played, these were pop tunes. Did you know the tunes before you went in the studio?
Did you have music, or did you --
No, you didn't know what you were going to do. You're standing there, and they come up, and they hand them out to Fats. Fats turn and put them on the piano, open them up.

Firsttime, and then he says, well, you know, now okay fellows, and he pass out a lead sheet to each one, to me, to Gene Sedric, guitar, you know, chords, maybe, or maybe a lead sheet, guitar, and to the bass. And when we hit (unintelligible) it had been -- uh, uh, some published -- you know what I'm trying to say, it was open --

Stock arrangement. First you see Fats hit the ceiling. 'No! Why did they do that? Bring me that bass part.' He would take it and change it. 'That's lousy,' you know. 'Who's doing this?' You know. That's the wrong bass, the wrong notes, because naturally the man would start playing what he sees, and a man like Billy Taylor, you know, he wasn't making a mistake.

'Oh After all, my, my, they'll never learn. Fats says bring me the part, and Fats would take it, and then he'd say play these notes, you know. And we'd make the record, and it would be beautiful, because they had the right notes, the right chords, and he knew. Believe me when I say he knew, he wasn't guessing. He knew.
